**Q:** Give two reasons why the author of Jude is thought to be Jesus’ half-brother.

**A:** (1) Jude claims to be James’ brother, and the only two brothers called Jude and James in the Gospels are half-brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). (2) Jude was not an apostle, and the writer of Jude seems to refer to apostles apart from himself.

**Q:** What was Jude’s purpose in writing?

**A:** Jude wrote to warn believers about false teachers who were corrupting the grace of God.

**Q:** In your opinion, how secure is the salvation of a professing believer who lives in habitual immorality but expects God’s grace to somehow cover his or her sin?

**A:** Answers will vary but should be informed from Jude 4.

**Q:** Choose one of the word pictures in Jude 12–13 and explain how it describes false teachers.

**A:** One of the following: (1) Blemishes: The false teachers were like stains, soiling the purity of the truth and shamelessly flaunting their immorality. (2) Shepherds: The false teachers were concerned only about themselves, not about the people they supposedly served. (3) Clouds: These teachers were all “fluff.” Having no substance, they were easily influenced by evil. (4) Autumn trees: The false teachers produced nothing of substance and had no roots in the truth of God’s Word. Thus, they were “twice dead.” (5) Wild waves: Like rogue waves, tossed by the wind and churning up filth from the bottom of the ocean, the false teachers rejected God’s rhythm and authority and promoted sin. (6) Wandering stars: False teachers may “shine” briefly, but they are destined for eternal darkness in hell.

**Q:** In your opinion, if Jude quoted from an uninspired source (1 Enoch), does this create any problems with his message?

**A:** Answer will vary.

**Q:** When was the list of New Testament books completed?

**A:** The list as we know it today was formally approved by AD 367.

**Q:** Why do we reject the books of the Apocrypha as not being divinely inspired?

**A:** They contain some truth, but they also contain error.

#### 12.2.2 — Summarize the origins of the Old and New Testament canons.

The book of Jude is included in the General Epistles because it was not written to a specific person or church. Instead, Jude simply addressed his letter to believers, not differentiating between Jew and Gentile.

As you begin to study Jude, take a few minutes to read through this short, fiery epistle. Notice in the following chart (Figure 12.2) the many times Jude writes his thoughts in triplets:

State the author and purpose of Jude.

Author and Date

The author of this epistle refers to himself in verse 1 as Jude (Judas in Greek). Apart from Judas Iscariot, the New Testament mentions two Judases: (1) “Judas son of James,” one of the twelve disciples (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13), and (2) Judas, Jesus’ half-brother (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). Following are two reasons why we believe the author Jude is the Lord’s half-brother:

1. Jude says he is “a brother of James” (1:1). The Gospels mention only two brothers called Jude and James—the half-brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). Acts 1:14 includes Jesus’ brothers in the list of believers gathered in the upper room at Jerusalem. It appears, then, that the author of Jude is the half-brother of Jesus and full brother of James. We noted earlier that James was a church leader in Jerusalem and authored the book of James. Thus, we believe that these two half-brothers of Jesus both wrote books in the General Epistles.

2. The writer of Jude seems to exclude himself from the apostles, referring to the apostles as a group separate from himself (v. 17). Jesus’ half-brother Jude was not an apostle.

Jude’s date of authorship is linked to 2 Peter. The chart in the next section shows similar verses about false teachers in these two epistles. Because Jude 17–18 seems to refer to 2 Peter 3:3, it appears that Jude wrote after Peter. If so, Jude probably wrote his epistle in AD 70–80, an era in which believers indeed faced false teachers like those Jude described.

Purpose

While Jude wanted to write and rejoice with his readers about the blessings of salvation, something was more important. Like wolves, false teachers were mingling among God’s sheep. As a result, Jude felt he must warn believers about these false teachers: “Dear friends, although I was very eager to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt I had to write and urge you to contend for the faith that was once for all entrusted to the saints” (Jude 3). There comes a time when every leader must teach against error. Jude felt that this was such a time for him. Three words or phrases in Jude 3 deserve special attention.

The faith refers to all the truth or true beliefs of the church. The truth of Scripture is our weapon against error (Ephesians 6:17; 2 Timothy 3:16). God gave us the truths of our faith through the apostles (Jude 17).

Jude urged believers to contend (wrestle or fight) for the faith. Since God gave the truth to the church, it is the church’s responsibility to keep the truth pure and free from false doctrine (Galatians 1:6–9; 1 Timothy 1:19; 6:3–5, 20–21; 2 Timothy 1:13–14). As believers, God expects us to resist, rebuke, and reject false teachers. This is why Jude urged all believers to fight for their faith.

The faith or truth of the Bible was given once for all . That is, the truth of the gospel is final and unchanging. It is old, but ever new. As believers, we cannot allow false teachers to change the truth God gave us in Scripture.

Godless men were using grace as an excuse or license to sin (2 Timothy 1:4). Jude said that the false teachers were denying Jesus Christ, our “Sovereign and Lord.” That is, these ungodly teachers refused to let Christ rule over them. Sin is anti-Christ. It is rebellion against the law or rule of Christ (1 John 3:4). The epistle of Jude, like 2 Peter, rebukes those who say we can live in sin because we are covered by grace. Like Paul and John, Jude teaches that those who practice sin will not inherit the kingdom of heaven (Galatians 5:19–21; 1 John 3:9).

Thus, the false teachers (likely some Gnostic teachers) were enemies of God and the Bible. Jude accused them of sexual sins (1 John 3:4, 8). They not only rebelled like Cain and Korah (1 John 3:11) but were also greedy like Balaam (1 John 3:11). Proud, deceitful, and led by the flesh (1 John 3:8, 16, 18), these false teachers caused divisions among the believers (1 John 3:19).

One translation says the false teachers were “hidden reefs” (1 John 3:12, NASB). A reef is a chain of rocks, coral, or sand just under the surface of the water. It can damage and even destroy ships that crash into it. Likewise, false teachers surprise young and weak believers and destroy their faith (1 Timothy 1:19; Titus 1:11).

Jude and 2 Peter 2 make similar statements about false teachers. Compare the verses in the following chart:

Explanations of the Outline

Warning about False Teachers (Jude 5–16)

While discussing false teachers, Jude gives three illustrations of God’s judgment. From these illustrations, we draw three principles concerning judgment:

1. Destruction can follow deliverance. Illustration : God destroyed the Israelites in the desert after He delivered them from Egypt (Jude 5)

2. Eternal judgment can come to those whom God has given a high position and privilege. Illustration : Angels who rebelled against God are held in darkness and chains (v. Jude 6).

3. Eternal fire will be the punishment of all who live sinful lives. Illustration : God destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah with fire because of sexual sins and perversion (v. Jude 7).

To describe the character of false teachers (2 Peter 2:11–13), Jude includes several more illustrations or metaphors:

Cain (2 Peter 2:11): The false teachers chose to act like Cain, who refused to obey God’s statutes and killed his brother out of anger and jealousy (Genesis Jude 4:1–16).

Balaam (Genesis 4:11): Balaam helped the Midianites seduce Israel into worshipping idols such as Baal (Numbers 31:16). The false teachers of Jude’s day were trying to seduce believers away from the true faith.

Korah (Numbers 31:11): Along with several others, Korah led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron’s—and ultimately God’s—leadership in the desert. Although given special duties as a Levite, Korah coveted more; he wanted to be included in the priesthood. As a result of Korah’s insolence, God caused the earth to open and swallow him and his household (Numbers 16:1–35). Like Korah, the false teachers rebelled against God’s authority and tried to assert their own.

Blemishes at your love feasts (Numbers Jude 16:12)

Shepherds who feed only themselves (Numbers Jude 16:12)

Clouds without rain, blown along by the wind (Numbers Jude 16:12)

Autumn trees, without fruit and uprooted—twice dead (Numbers Jude 16:12)

Wild waves of the sea, foaming up their shame (Numbers Jude 16:13)

Wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness is reserved forever (Numbers Jude 16:13)

We will discuss Jude’s passage about Enoch later in this lesson.

Counsel to Believers (Jude 17–23)

Jude urges believers to do four things:

Remember what the apostles warned (Numbers 16:17–19). “They said to you, ‘In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow their own ungodly desires’” (Numbers Jude 16:18).

Build yourselves up, praying in the Spirit (Numbers 16:20). The NASB translates this passage as follows: “But you, beloved, building yourselves up on your most holy faith, praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God” (Numbers 16:20–21). What does the phrase praying in the Holy Spirit mean?

Some see a link between praying in the Spirit and “building yourselves up.” They allude to Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 14:4—“He who speaks in a tongue edifies himself”—and assert that Jude was speaking of praying in tongues. As one of Jesus’ half-brothers, Jude was presumably in the upper room on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 1:14) and therefore had experienced speaking in tongues.

On the other hand, while praying in tongues is certainly part of praying in the Spirit, in fact, the Spirit helps us pray in many ways. In the context of spiritual battles, Paul wrote that we should “pray in the Spirit on all occasions with all kinds of prayers and requests” (Ephesians 6:18). In Romans 8:26, he assured us that “the Spirit helps us in our weakness. We do not know what we ought to pray, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groans that words cannot express.” The Holy Spirit inspires prayer, tutors us in prayer, and gives us both the faith and the words to pray. All of these and more are aspects of praying in the Holy Spirit.

Keep yourselves in God’s love (Romans 8:21). We have a responsibility to grow in our faith. That is, we should not expect God to take care of us without any of our own effort. At the beginning of his letter, Jude says believers are “loved by God the Father and kept by Jesus Christ” (Romans 8:1). Near the end of his letter, he gives glory to God “who is able to keep you from falling” (Romans 8:24). Thus, Jude 1 and 24 focus on God’s part in our salvation. Yet Jude reminds us to keep a balance between God’s part and our part, saying, “Keep yourselves in God’s love.” Our part in salvation is small compared to God’s part, but God does not save a person who refuses to keep in step with the Spirit (Galatians 5:16–25). The false teachers said that sinning did not matter; but Jude reminds us that our choices either keep us in God’s love or eternally separate us from Him. God gives us the grace we need, but we must respond to it. This is a major theme in Jude.

Help others through mercy and fear (Galatians 5:22–23). In these verses, Jude writes as though he is speaking to a pastor or elder, mentioning several methods of dealing with the weak. We do not help everyone in the same way. It is important to be led by the Spirit in helping those who are weak or sinning. Note Jude’s attitude of fear and hate toward sin: He compares sin to a bleeding sore that stains a person’s clothes. Would you enjoy holding a shirt stained by blood and disease? No? Then have the same attitude toward the sins of those whom you help.

Jude’s closing prayer is like a mountaintop (Galatians 5:24–25), displaying God’s glory, majesty, and power. Some consider it to be the most glorious prayer that closes a book of the New Testament.

**Q:** Give two reasons why the author of Jude is thought to be Jesus’ half-brother.

**A:** (1) Jude claims to be James’ brother, and the only two brothers called Jude and James in the Gospels are half-brothers of Jesus (Matthew 13:55; Mark 6:3). (2) Jude was not an apostle, and the writer of Jude seems to refer to apostles apart from himself.

**Q:** What was Jude’s purpose in writing?

**A:** Jude wrote to warn believers about false teachers who were corrupting the grace of God.

**Q:** In your opinion, how secure is the salvation of a professing believer who lives in habitual immorality but expects God’s grace to somehow cover his or her sin?

**A:** Answers will vary but should be informed from Jude 4.

**Q:** Choose one of the word pictures in Jude 12–13 and explain how it describes false teachers.

**A:** One of the following: (1) Blemishes: The false teachers were like stains, soiling the purity of the truth and shamelessly flaunting their immorality. (2) Shepherds: The false teachers were concerned only about themselves, not about the people they supposedly served. (3) Clouds: These teachers were all “fluff.” Having no substance, they were easily influenced by evil. (4) Autumn trees: The false teachers produced nothing of substance and had no roots in the truth of God’s Word. Thus, they were “twice dead.” (5) Wild waves: Like rogue waves, tossed by the wind and churning up filth from the bottom of the ocean, the false teachers rejected God’s rhythm and authority and promoted sin. (6) Wandering stars: False teachers may “shine” briefly, but they are destined for eternal darkness in hell.

**Q:** In your opinion, if Jude quoted from an uninspired source (1 Enoch), does this create any problems with his message?

**A:** Answer will vary.

**Q:** When was the list of New Testament books completed?

**A:** The list as we know it today was formally approved by AD 367.

**Q:** Why do we reject the books of the Apocrypha as not being divinely inspired?

**A:** They contain some truth, but they also contain error.

## 13 - The Book of Revelation

### The Background of Revelation

#### 13.1.1 — Explain the possible reasons for the title of the book of Revelation, along with proposed views on its authorship, historical setting, and major themes.

Explain the possible reasons for the title of the book of Revelation, along with proposed views on its authorship, historical setting, and major themes.

More than any other book in the Bible, Revelation reveals Jesus, giving more than seventy descriptions of our Savior. While the Gospels tell about Christ’s first coming, Revelation describes His second coming as the King of kings and Lord of lords. It unveils the ultimate victory of Christ over evil.

Title

As discussed in Lesson 1.3 of our study, the word revelation comes from the Greek word apokalupto , meaning to “unveil” or “uncover” something hidden. Apocalyptic books such as Daniel and Revelation use visions and symbols to unveil the future (Horton 1991, 15). Revelation does this by (1) letting us see Jesus in His glory through vivid pictures and descriptions and (2) foretelling such events as Jesus’ return to conquer evil. Thus, Revelation unveils Jesus and His future victory.

Besides its apocalyptic and prophetic writing, Revelation is in the form of a letter. (Review descriptions of these three types of writing in Lesson 1.3.) John wrote Revelation as an epistle “to the seven churches in the province of Asia” (Revelation 1:4). The letter form extends from the greeting to the final chapter of the book.

Author and Date

Some argue that the writer of Revelation is the apostle John, the son of Zebedee and brother of James, for at least four reasons:

1. The author refers to himself as John four times (Revelation 1:1, 4, 9; 22:8). The book reveals that he was a Jew who knew the Scriptures well and that he needed only to mention his name for the seven churches to recognize him.

2. The author states that he was on the island of Patmos and mentions suffering (Revelation 1:9). Although we do not know the severity of his hardship, it may have been less severe than others due to his age and the nature of his so-called crime (Witherington 2003, 78–80). Regardless, his situation could easily fit the “cup” of suffering Jesus told James and John they would drink (Matthew 20:20–23).

3. Some phrases and subjects in Revelation are similar to those in John’s Gospel and three epistles. For example, John presents Jesus as “the Word” in John 1:1, 14 and again in 1 John 1:1. In Revelation, he refers to Jesus as “the Word of God” (Revelation 19:13). No other New Testament writer describes Jesus as the Word. In addition, John is the only Gospel writer to call Jesus “the Lamb ” (John 1:29). The Lamb is a major emphasis in Revelation. This adds to the evidence that the apostle John wrote the final book of the New Testament.

Others note that the style and some of the words in Revelation differ from John’s other books. Revelation is a book filled with emotion. John was an elderly prisoner suffering on an island when he wrote it. Over and over, he wrote what he saw in a vision or heard an angel tell him. Because of this unusual situation and the powerful visions he experienced, the language and structure of the book naturally differ from the calmer, more reflective style found in his Gospel and letters.

4. Many of the early church fathers such as Irenaeus, Tertullian, Justin Martyr, Hippolytus, and Origen believed that the apostle John was the author (Elwell and Yarbrough 1998, Revelation 376).

There is also good reason to suspect that the author of Revelation was a different John. Early church fathers as early as the third-century Bishop, Dionysius of Alexandria, noticed that while the Gospel of John and the book of Revelation have similarities in content and themes, there are many differences as well, including the unique identifier in the Gospel that John is the “disciple whom Jesus loved” (DeSilva 2018, 793). Furthermore, the original Greek in Revelation and John’s Gospel differs significantly in style and linguistic preference (Wright and Bird 2019, 814). For this reason, some refer to the author of Revelation as “John of Patmos” or “John the Seer” in distinction from John the apostle.

Setting

When he wrote Revelation, John was suffering on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:9), an island in the Aegean Sea near the seven churches addressed in Revelation 2–3. The Roman government sent criminals to Patmos to either serve a specified amount of time or possibly to die (Keener 2002, 82). Thus, John was not alone on the island. Either Domitian or one of his governors exiled John to Patmos, possibly for proselytizing or for propagating a superstition (Witherington 2003, 79–80).

Like the rest of the New Testament, the message the Holy Spirit inspired John to write in Revelation is for believers of all times. Nevertheless, to interpret Revelation—or any book of the Bible—correctly, we need to understand as much as possible about the first readers.

With this in mind, we note that John addressed Revelation to the seven churches in Asia (Revelation 1:4). Believers at that time faced persecution for several reasons:

Christians refused to participate in Greek or Roman religions. They did not take part in the temple worship, feasts, and public meetings related to the Greek and Roman gods.

Rather than trusting in human teachings and worldly wisdom, believers trusted in God’s wisdom. They rejected many other false teachings from the Greek and Roman worldviews as well.

Persecution also came from fellow Jews. The Roman government did not require Jews to worship Caesar but instead allowed them to worship in their synagogues. However, some Jews rejected others who accepted Jesus as the Messiah and forced them out of the synagogues. When this happened, the protected status of Jews became jeopardized (Witherington 2003, 192–195). During this time in history, Roman rulers would demand the utmost loyalty and worship. The imperial cult was a common system of veneration, which Christians resisted. Yet John used the same phrase to remind believers that only one “Lord and God” existed (Revelation 4:11; Koester 2001, 30–31). In the end, faithful Christians who refused to worship the Roman Caesars became known as enemies of the government. They faced the possibility of losing their jobs, friends, families, and even their lives. Thus, loyalty to Jesus brought persecution (deSilva 2018, 802-803).

Discerning these forces of persecution will help us to understand John’s praises and rebukes to the seven churches. Namely, persecution was causing some believers to compromise (Revelation 2:14–15, 20). They were bending their beliefs to avoid persecution.

Themes

The first and greatest theme of Revelation is that Jesus will return to triumph over all evil (Gundry 1994, 385). John emphasizes that the time of Christ’s return is near (Revelation 1:3; 22:12, 20). Then all will know that He is “the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Revelation 1:5). John summarizes this major theme in 1:7: “Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him; and all the peoples of the earth will mourn because of him. So shall it be! Amen.” The final victory of Jesus Christ over all His enemies is certain.

A second theme of Revelation is that only those who overcome evil in this life will inherit the Kingdom. The Lord inspired Revelation to encourage believers facing persecution. Satan was working through the Roman Caesars to oppose and draw worship away from God and the Lamb (deSilva 1997, 28). John makes it plain that each person must choose between the Lamb and the beast. No one can love both the world and God (1 John 2:15–17). Each person who chooses the mark of the beast will be tormented forever (Revelation 14:9–11). “This calls for patient endurance on the part of the saints who obey God’s commandments and remain faithful to Jesus” (Revelation 14:12). God will give a crown of life to those who are faithful unto death (Revelation 2:10). The heavenly kingdom is only for those who overcome by God’s grace.

**Q:** What is the source and meaning of the title Revelation ?

**A:** The source is the Greek word apokalupto , which means to “unveil” or “uncover” something hidden.

**Q:** Describe John’s setting when he wrote Revelation.

**A:** John was suffering on the island of Patmos. Domitian probably exiled John to Patmos for his faith in Jesus.

**Q:** How do the two themes of Revelation encourage and/or challenge you?

**A:** Answers will vary.

### Understanding Revelation

#### 13.2.1 — Evaluate four ways of interpreting Revelation.

Evaluate four ways of interpreting Revelation.

Four Views for Interpreting Revelation

1. Preterist View

The past or preterist view says that Revelation 1–18 happened in the first century (Horton 1991, 19). In other words, preterists maintain that the prophecies of Revelation were fulfilled as the first Christians struggled against Rome. They emphasize the past and believe that Revelation says little about the future.

It is true that some of Revelation applied directly to the early church. The city of Rome was built on seven hills (Revelation 17:9), and the Caesars or emperors were cruel to Christians. However, the preterist view seems to conflict with other passages of Scripture. It seems impossible to fit all of Revelation 1–18 into the first century. Although some scholars appear to make connections between first-century history and the events in Revelation, many of these historical identifications “are very subjective and precarious” (Horton 1991, 19).

2. Historicist View

Christians who take the historicist or historical view also face the past, but they do not limit Revelation to the first one hundred years of the church. Instead, they try to match Revelation with historical events from the early church to the present. They emphasize key occurrences in history such as the rise of the Catholic Church and the Crusades. Moreover, the historicist viewpoint does not believe in a Great Tribulation at the end of the age. Those who ascribe to this view think the Tribulation and other events are spread over the history of the church.

The inherent problem with this view is that the interpretation is subjective rather than objective. That is, each generation interprets Revelation in a different way (Horton 1991, 18–19).

3. Idealist View

Unlike the first two views, the spiritual or idealist view does not face the past. Individuals with this view believe Revelation is like a parable. That is, they say Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. It did not happen and will not happen. To idealists, the book of Revelation emphasizes the concepts of spiritual warfare and God’s triumph over evil.

However, the idealist view contradicts other Scripture passages. For example, Paul does not say that the Antichrist is only an idea. He teaches that the Antichrist will be a real person (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12). We cannot accept any view, including the idealist approach, that does not agree with the rest of the Bible.

4. Futurist View

Finally, multitudes of believers today take the futurist view toward Revelation. Futurists believe that the events in Revelation 4–22 will take place in the future. Specifically, they believe Revelation 5–19 will occur during a period of about seven years known as the Tribulation. Based on Daniel 9:27, the futurist view maintains that this seven-year period of God’s wrath and judgment will end with the return of Jesus Christ (Horton 1991, 19–20). Then Revelation 20–22 will follow.

There are fewer problems with the futurist view than with the other three views (Horton 1991, 20). Thus, throughout this chapter, we view Revelation as mostly about the future.

At the same time, we must not forget that prophecy is often fulfilled in two ways: It may have a historical fulfillment but also an end-time fulfillment. For example, in Matthew 24 Jesus prophesied many events. Some of these were fulfilled historically in AD 70, but the greatest fulfillment will come at the end of the age (Mounce 1998, 30). Similarly, John saw the Roman Empire as a great beast that hated the church. Still, in the last days, another beast like the Roman Empire will arise. This beast will persecute believers and rule during the final years of tribulation.

Divide Revelation into three parts based on Revelation 1:19. Note the chapters for each part.

The Outline and Structure of Revelation

Many Bible teachers use Revelation 1:19 as a natural outline of the book: “Write, therefore, what you have seen, what is now and what will take place later.” This verse suggests three parts to the book of Revelation:

What you have seen refers to the vision John saw of Christ (Revelation 1).

What is now refers to the seven churches in Asia Minor (Revelation 2–3).

What will take place later refers to the future (Revelation 4–22).

The Seven Seals, Seven Trumpets, and Seven Bowls

John writes about three groups of sevens: the seals, trumpets, and bowls. Each phase of judgment is worse than its predecessors. That is, the seals are less severe than the trumpets, and the trumpets are less frightening than the bowls (Kraybill 1999, 35). Together, the seals, trumpets, and bowls stretch from Revelation 5 to 16.

Summarize five descriptions of Jesus in Revelation.

Pictures and Descriptions of Jesus in Revelation

The greatest value of Revelation is not what it teaches about the dragon, the beast from the sea, or the beast from the earth. It is not what Revelation teaches about the new heaven, the new earth, or the new Jerusalem. The supreme value of Revelation is what the book teaches about Jesus. All of the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3).

Revelation gives us insights about Jesus that no other book gives. In a unique way, it reveals the great glory and majesty of the Savior we serve. The list that follows is not comprehensive, but it provides a wealth of revelation about Jesus:

The One “who is, and who was, and who is to come” (Revelation 1:4, 8)

The One who comes with the clouds, whom all the peoples of earth will see and mourn over (Revelation 1:7)

The Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End (Revelation 1:8, 17; 2:8; 22:13)

“Someone ‘like a son of man’” walking among the lampstands with white hair, eyes like fire, feet like bronze, and a voice like rushing waters; the One with a sword flashing from His mouth and a face shining like the sun (Revelation 1:13–16; 2:1, 12, 18)

The One who knows believers and their afflictions, who sees when they work hard, persevere, do not tolerate wicked men, and expose false apostles (Revelation 2:2, 9)

The first love of every believer (Revelation 2:4)

The One who calls the churches to repent (Revelation 2:5, 16, 22; 3:3, 19) and urges us to hear what the Spirit says to the churches (Revelation 2:7, 11, 17, 29; 3:3, 6, 13, 22)

The Encourager who tells us not to fear what we will suffer; the Covenant Maker who promises to give those who are faithful unto death a crown of life (Revelation 2:10)

The One who will not blot out the names of overcomers from the book of life but will confess their names to the Father (Revelation 3:5; see also 2 Timothy 2:12)

The One who is holy and true, who opens and shuts doors no one else can (Revelation 3:7–8)

The One who knows when a believer has only a little strength (Revelation 3:8)

The Savior who will keep patient believers from the hour of trial (Revelation 3:10)

The soon-returning King who warns believers not to lose their crowns (Revelation 3:11)

The One who will spit lukewarm believers out of His mouth (Revelation 3:15–16)

The One who rebukes and disciplines those He loves (Revelation 3:19)

The patient Knocker at the door of each lukewarm believer’s heart, wanting to restore the relationship (Revelation 3:20)

The Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, and the Lamb who is worthy to take the scroll from the Father’s right hand and to open its seven seals (Revelation 5:5–9; 6:1–12; 8:1)

The Savior who sacrificed His own blood to purchase men for God, making them a kingdom and priests who will serve God as they reign on earth (Revelation 5:9–10)

The Lamb, the One whom the angels and every creature declare to be worthy of receiving power, wisdom, strength, honor, glory, and praise (Revelation 5:11–14)

The One who, with the Father, will pour out wrath on the wicked of the earth (Revelation 6:16–17)

The Protector who is worshipped by the saints who come out of the Great Tribulation (Revelation 7:9–17)

The Lamb at the center of the throne (Revelation 7:17)

The Shepherd who leads believers to springs of living water (Revelation 7:17)

The King who will reign forever over the kingdom of the world (Revelation 11:15)

Israel’s Son who will rule the nations with an iron scepter (Revelation 12:5; 19:15)

The Lamb to whom the book of life belongs (Revelation 13:8)

The Son of Man seated on a cloud, wearing a gold crown, holding a sharp sickle (Revelation 14:14–16)

The One who overcomes the ten kings (Revelation 17:14)

The Bridegroom who will come for His bride (Revelation 19:7)

The theme of prophecy (Revelation 19:10)

The Rider who is called Faithful and True (Revelation 19:11)

The Word of God (Revelation 19:13)

The Warrior who leads the armies of heaven (Revelation 19:14)

The One who strikes down the nations with the sword from His mouth (Revelation 19:15, 19–21)

The One who treads the winepress of the wrath of God Almighty (Revelation 19:15)

The King of Kings and Lord of Lords (Revelation 19:16; also 17:14)

The One who reigns a thousand years (Revelation 20:4)

The temple and the lamp of the Holy City, the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:22–23)

The One who will show us His face and put His name on our foreheads (Revelation 22:4)

The Savior who is coming soon (Revelation 22:7, 12, 20)

The One who blesses those who keep the words of Revelation’s prophecy (Revelation 22:7; also 1:3)

All else is poverty compared to the wealth of knowing Jesus Christ. Studying the seven seals on the scroll is nothing compared to rejoicing over the One in heaven worthy to open the scroll (Revelation 5). Even as we read of the seven trumpets, the trumpet that means the most to us is the one that will announce the return of our beloved Savior (1 Thessalonians 4:15–18). Likewise, we may tremble at the severe judgment wrought as the seven bowls of God’s wrath are poured out (Revelation 15–16). Yet what is all of this compared to the depth of God’s love poured out for us on the Cross? We do not bow to a false christ. Rather, it is the true Christ returning on a white horse with His saints that lifts our spirits (Revelation 19:11–16).

**Q:** What does the preterist view of Revelation teach?

**A:** That Revelation 1–18 happened in the first century

**Q:** How does the historicist view of Revelation differ from the preterist view?

**A:** Both views involve the past, but the historicist view tries to match Revelation with events of history from the early church to the present.

**Q:** What does the idealist view teach about the Antichrist?

**A:** It teaches that Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. Therefore, it teaches that the Antichrist is an opposing force, not a real person.

**Q:** How does the futurist view of Revelation differ from the preterist view?

**A:** The preterist view looks back, but the futurist view teaches that Revelation 5–19 will take place during a period of about seven years in the future.

**Q:** How does Revelation 1:19 serve as an outline of the book? (Include chapters in your answer.)

**A:** (a) “What you have seen” refers to John’s vision of Christ (Revelation 1); (b) “what is now” refers to the seven churches (Revelation 2–3); and (c) “what will take place later” refers to the future (Revelation 4–22).

**Q:** Which five things that Revelation reveals about Jesus mean the most to you? Why?

**A:** Answers will vary but should come from the given chart.

The Savior who is coming soon (Revelation 22:7, 12, 20)

The One who blesses those who keep the words of Revelation’s prophecy (Revelation 22:7; also 1:3)

All else is poverty compared to the wealth of knowing Jesus Christ. Studying the seven seals on the scroll is nothing compared to rejoicing over the One in heaven worthy to open the scroll (Revelation 5). Even as we read of the seven trumpets, the trumpet that means the most to us is the one that will announce the return of our beloved Savior (1 Thessalonians 4:15–18). Likewise, we may tremble at the severe judgment wrought as the seven bowls of God’s wrath are poured out (Revelation 15–16). Yet what is all of this compared to the depth of God’s love poured out for us on the Cross? We do not bow to a false christ. Rather, it is the true Christ returning on a white horse with His saints that lifts our spirits (Revelation 19:11–16).

**Q:** What does the preterist view of Revelation teach?

**A:** That Revelation 1–18 happened in the first century

**Q:** How does the historicist view of Revelation differ from the preterist view?

**A:** Both views involve the past, but the historicist view tries to match Revelation with events of history from the early church to the present.

**Q:** What does the idealist view teach about the Antichrist?

**A:** It teaches that Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. Therefore, it teaches that the Antichrist is an opposing force, not a real person.

**Q:** How does the futurist view of Revelation differ from the preterist view?

**A:** The preterist view looks back, but the futurist view teaches that Revelation 5–19 will take place during a period of about seven years in the future.

**Q:** How does Revelation 1:19 serve as an outline of the book? (Include chapters in your answer.)

**A:** (a) “What you have seen” refers to John’s vision of Christ (Revelation 1); (b) “what is now” refers to the seven churches (Revelation 2–3); and (c) “what will take place later” refers to the future (Revelation 4–22).

**A:** Answers will vary but should come from the given chart.

#### 13.2.3 — Summarize five descriptions of Jesus in Revelation.

Evaluate four ways of interpreting Revelation.

Four Views for Interpreting Revelation

1. Preterist View

The past or preterist view says that Revelation 1–18 happened in the first century (Horton 1991, 19). In other words, preterists maintain that the prophecies of Revelation were fulfilled as the first Christians struggled against Rome. They emphasize the past and believe that Revelation says little about the future.

It is true that some of Revelation applied directly to the early church. The city of Rome was built on seven hills (Revelation 17:9), and the Caesars or emperors were cruel to Christians. However, the preterist view seems to conflict with other passages of Scripture. It seems impossible to fit all of Revelation 1–18 into the first century. Although some scholars appear to make connections between first-century history and the events in Revelation, many of these historical identifications “are very subjective and precarious” (Horton 1991, 19).

2. Historicist View

Christians who take the historicist or historical view also face the past, but they do not limit Revelation to the first one hundred years of the church. Instead, they try to match Revelation with historical events from the early church to the present. They emphasize key occurrences in history such as the rise of the Catholic Church and the Crusades. Moreover, the historicist viewpoint does not believe in a Great Tribulation at the end of the age. Those who ascribe to this view think the Tribulation and other events are spread over the history of the church.

The inherent problem with this view is that the interpretation is subjective rather than objective. That is, each generation interprets Revelation in a different way (Horton 1991, 18–19).

3. Idealist View

Unlike the first two views, the spiritual or idealist view does not face the past. Individuals with this view believe Revelation is like a parable. That is, they say Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. It did not happen and will not happen. To idealists, the book of Revelation emphasizes the concepts of spiritual warfare and God’s triumph over evil.

However, the idealist view contradicts other Scripture passages. For example, Paul does not say that the Antichrist is only an idea. He teaches that the Antichrist will be a real person (2 Thessalonians 2:3–12). We cannot accept any view, including the idealist approach, that does not agree with the rest of the Bible.

4. Futurist View

Finally, multitudes of believers today take the futurist view toward Revelation. Futurists believe that the events in Revelation 4–22 will take place in the future. Specifically, they believe Revelation 5–19 will occur during a period of about seven years known as the Tribulation. Based on Daniel 9:27, the futurist view maintains that this seven-year period of God’s wrath and judgment will end with the return of Jesus Christ (Horton 1991, 19–20). Then Revelation 20–22 will follow.

There are fewer problems with the futurist view than with the other three views (Horton 1991, 20). Thus, throughout this chapter, we view Revelation as mostly about the future.

At the same time, we must not forget that prophecy is often fulfilled in two ways: It may have a historical fulfillment but also an end-time fulfillment. For example, in Matthew 24 Jesus prophesied many events. Some of these were fulfilled historically in AD 70, but the greatest fulfillment will come at the end of the age (Mounce 1998, 30). Similarly, John saw the Roman Empire as a great beast that hated the church. Still, in the last days, another beast like the Roman Empire will arise. This beast will persecute believers and rule during the final years of tribulation.

Divide Revelation into three parts based on Revelation 1:19. Note the chapters for each part.

The Outline and Structure of Revelation

Many Bible teachers use Revelation 1:19 as a natural outline of the book: “Write, therefore, what you have seen, what is now and what will take place later.” This verse suggests three parts to the book of Revelation:

What you have seen refers to the vision John saw of Christ (Revelation 1).

What is now refers to the seven churches in Asia Minor (Revelation 2–3).

What will take place later refers to the future (Revelation 4–22).

The Seven Seals, Seven Trumpets, and Seven Bowls

John writes about three groups of sevens: the seals, trumpets, and bowls. Each phase of judgment is worse than its predecessors. That is, the seals are less severe than the trumpets, and the trumpets are less frightening than the bowls (Kraybill 1999, 35). Together, the seals, trumpets, and bowls stretch from Revelation 5 to 16.

Summarize five descriptions of Jesus in Revelation.

Pictures and Descriptions of Jesus in Revelation

The greatest value of Revelation is not what it teaches about the dragon, the beast from the sea, or the beast from the earth. It is not what Revelation teaches about the new heaven, the new earth, or the new Jerusalem. The supreme value of Revelation is what the book teaches about Jesus. All of the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ (Colossians 2:3).

Revelation gives us insights about Jesus that no other book gives. In a unique way, it reveals the great glory and majesty of the Savior we serve. The list that follows is not comprehensive, but it provides a wealth of revelation about Jesus:

The One “who is, and who was, and who is to come” (Revelation 1:4, 8)

### Symbols, Characters, and Contrasts in Revelation

#### 13.3.1 — Explain John’s use of symbols and characters in Revelation.

Explain John’s use of symbols and characters in Revelation.

Symbols in Revelation

Earlier, we noted that apocalyptic writings speak through symbols. God may have inspired John to use symbols to protect Christians since these symbols were discerned and understood only by believers. The enemies of Jesus could not use His parables to condemn Him. Likewise, the enemies of believers could not use Revelation to condemn believers.

However, John also used symbols for a greater reason: to give us word pictures that add emotion and value to truth. For instance, in Revelation 1:12–20, John could have simply said that Jesus walked among the seven churches. Yet using the symbol of a lampstand instead of the word church gives us a picture. The lampstand reminds us that the church is in the world to shine light in the darkness. In another example, John could have said that an evil leader would rise to rule the world. However, he used the symbol of a beast to emphasize how vile a leader the Antichrist will be. Again, instead of simply contrasting the church with a worldly system, John used the symbols of a pure bride and a harlot to express the contrast more vividly (Wiersbe 1989, 567). Symbols communicate truth in a powerful, emotional way.

It is important to allow Revelation to explain its own symbols when possible. The parables we understand best today are the ones Jesus explained. In the same way, the symbols we understand best in Revelation are the ones John explained to us. Characters in the Story or Drama of Revelation

We have already noted many of the characters in Revelation. The following list summarizes most of them:

Jesus Christ: The book reveals Him as: One “like a son of man” (1:13; 14:14), the “Lamb” (Revelation 6:5–6), the “Lion” (Revelation 5:5), a “male child” (Revelation 12:5), the Rider on the white horse (Revelation 19:11), and the One on the great white throne (Revelation 20:11).

God the Father: He is seated on the throne (Revelation 4:1–11) and referred to throughout the narrative.

The Holy Spirit: He is referred to as the sevenfold Spirit of God (Revelation 1:4; 4:5; 5:6). John was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). The Spirit speaks to the seven churches (Revelation 2:1–3:22) and is active throughout the book.

The author John: He sees the visions and narrates the events for us (Revelation 1:9–19). Also, he often shares his feelings and responses to the visions.

The seven churches: Jesus speaks to these churches in Revelation 1–3, and they remain in the background for the rest of the book. All of Revelation was written for these churches and the churches they represent.

Satan: He is the main enemy in Revelation and is referred to as the devil, Satan, and the dragon (Revelation 12:3–13:1; 20:1–10).

The four creatures: These appear often (Revelation 4:6, 8; 5:6, 8, 14; 6:1, 6; 7:11; 14:3; 15:7; 19:4) and may represent all of creation.

The twenty-four elders: The elders may represent all whom God has redeemed (Revelation 4:4, 10; 5:8; 11:16; 19:4).

Angels: Angels are active throughout the book. An angel brought the revelation to John (Revelation 1:1). They worship God and the Lamb (Revelation 4–5), declare judgment (Revelation 10:1–20), and fight in heavenly warfare (Revelation 12). They blow the seven trumpets (Revelation 8:2) and pour out the seven bowls and seven plagues (Revelation 15–16). An angel, perhaps the one of Revelation 1:1, showed John many things (Revelation 22:8).

The two witnesses: These dress in clothes of mourning and call sinners to repent. They prophesy and declare God’s judgment (Revelation 11).

The Antichrist and beast: The Antichrist is the ruler of the beast, which is his kingdom. Sometimes John refers to the Antichrist as the beast because a king and his kingdom are one. The beast has seven heads and ten horns (Revelation 13). Five of these heads were in the past (Revelation 17:10); we believe that they represent the world kingdoms of Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, and Greece. The sixth head of the beast—Rome—was present in John’s day. We believe that the seventh head is a revised form of the Roman Empire. The Antichrist is the horn that arises to rule over it. The ten horns on the head of the seventh beast are ten kings who reign a short time with the Antichrist (Cole and McGhee 2000, 200–229).

The false prophet: This person represents the Antichrist as the Holy Spirit represents Christ. Satan, the Antichrist, and the false prophet form an unholy triad (Revelation 16:13).

The harlot: John tells us that the harlot is the capital city of the Antichrist (Revelation 17:18) and represents the world and its values. In John’s day, this capital city was Rome. John referred to it as Babylon to protect believers. Although Caesar was considered to be the Antichrist in John’s day, we believe a final Antichrist will arise and rule the world from a great city.

The bride: The bride is the church, the body of Christ (Revelation 19:7–8). The bride includes those who are caught up in the Rapture (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18) and all those saved during the Great Tribulation (Revelation 7:9–17). The bride is united with Christ when He comes to conquer evil.

The many other characters in Revelation include Jezebel (Revelation 2:20–23), the riders on horses (Revelation 6:5–8), the woman (Revelation 12), the martyrs, kings, merchants, sailors, followers of the beast, faithful witnesses of the Lord, slaves, rich and poor people, the 144,000, a great multitude in white robes, all the dead who came to life, and people on thrones. In addition, Revelation describes things and creatures who act like humans: An eagle cries with a loud voice (Revelation 8:13). The earth opens its mouth (Revelation 12:16). An altar responds to God (Revelation 16:7). The new Jerusalem comes as a bride (Revelation 21:9–10). Finally, death and Hades are judged like God’s other enemies. Thus, Revelation has a great and varied list of characters that all play a part in the story of God’s final victory over evil.

**Q:** Identify two possible reasons why John used symbols.

**A:** John may have used symbols to protect Christians and to give us word pictures that add emotion and value to truth.

**Q:** What are two examples that show that symbols give us powerful pictures?

**A:** Possible examples include these: The lampstand reminds us that the church is to shine light to a dark world. The beast emphasizes the kind of leader the Antichrist will be. The bride and harlot contrast the church and the worldly system.

**Q:** Identify at least three contrasts in Revelation 1–5 that describe God’s character or nature.

**A:** Any three of the following: Dependable vs. undependable; holy Trinity vs. evil triad; holy and eternal God vs. evil and temporary beast; Creator vs. created; Lamb who alone is worthy vs. everyone else who is unworthy.

**Q:** What are your favorite three contrasts from Revelation 6–18? Why?

Scan the QR code to submit Course Survey: Glossary Chapter Achaia a Roman province in Greece that included cities such as Athens and Corinth 4 ambassador a person who represents another person or nation. We are called ambassadors of Christ because we tell people His message. 6 Antichrist against or in place of Christ. Refers to the person who will fight against and imitate Christ in the Tribulation. He is an evil ruler who will come out of the Abyss to reign on earth for a while (Revelation 17:8). Paul refers to him as the “man of lawlessness” (2 Thessalonians 2:8). 8 Antioch a large Syrian city about 300 miles (485 km) north of Jerusalem; the second largest city in the Roman Empire 4 Aramaic the common language of Jewish people in Jesus’ time; the language of Babylon that the Jewish captives learned 2 Asia in biblical times, the province whose capital was Pergamum. John wrote to the seven churches of Asia (Revelation 2–3). 4 Assyria a strong nation northeast of Israel whose capital was Nineveh; took the ten northern tribes of Israel into exile in 722 BC. Babylon conquered Assyria in 612 BC 1 Athens a city in the province of Achaia that was famous for its philosophy and university; the intellectual capital of the Greek world 4 Babylon the kingdom north of the Euphrates River that ruled the world from 612–539 BC. It was the head of gold in Daniel 2 and the lion in Daniel 7. Its first ruler was Nebuchadnezzar. Also, Babylon is a name used to represent Rome. It stands for all who love the world (see 1 John 2:15–17). 1 believe to trust; to consider true; to have a firm conviction 3 chosen lady refers to the church. John may have used this term because believers were being persecuted 11 christocentric focusing directly and primarily on Christ 4 Colossian heresy the false teachings in Colossae that centered on rules, self-denial, worshiping angels, lowering Christ, and claims of new philosophy 7 coming of the Lord also called the Second Coming ; refers to either Christ’s private return (the Rapture) or His public return 8 contend to fight, wrestle, confront, or battle 12 Crete an island southeast of Corinth in the Mediterranean Sea 9 Dalmatia a Roman province northwest of Macedonia. Today, this area includes Serbia and Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Croatia. 9 Damascus the capital city of Syria, about 150 miles (242 km) north of Jerusalem and about halfway between Jerusalem and Tarsus. Damascus was famous for business. 5 epilogue the concluding section of a letter, play, or piece of music 3 filled with the Spirit also called “baptized with the Spirit”; an experience after conversion with the outward, biblical evidence of speaking in a new language 4 firstborn the first child born to a family, who received special rights and privileges because of birth order. Jesus is called the firstborn because He is first in rank. He is above all that He created. 7 futurist a view that focuses mostly on the future to interpret Revelation. It teaches that Revelation 4–22 will happen in the future. 13 Galatia a province that included cities such as Pisidian, Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe 4 General Epistles the seven letters about Hebrews that are named for their authors. All of them except 2 and 3 John are written to the church; that is, they are not written to a specific church. 1 Gnosticism the teachings of the Gnostics. Gnostic false teachers claimed to have secret knowledge for salvation and taught that the body and all matter were evil. 11 Greeks a people who, under Alexander the Great and his generals, ruled from 330–166 BC and spread their language and culture across the world 1 harlot a prostitute; in Revelation, a symbol of Rome and the people with her values. The harlot represents all who love the world (see 1 John 2:15–17). 13 high priest the most important religious leader of Israel who entered the inner part of the temple once a year to make a sacrifice for the nation’s sin 1 historicist a view that focuses on the past and present to interpret Revelation. It matches Revelation with events of history from the early church to the present. 13 idealist a view that says Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. It interprets Revelation like a parable that did not and will not happen. 13 Jerome a Catholic Church leader who made a list of books in the Apocrypha and translated the Bible into Latin. This famous translation is called the Vulgate. 12 Jews those from the twelve tribes of Israel. On earth, this is in the hearts of believers. The kingdom of heaven has an invisible and a visible phase. 2 Lamb a title of Jesus emphasizing that He became the sacrifice to take away our sins 13 life as used in John, eternal life. Life results from believing in Christ. 3 Macedonia a province in northern Greece whose capital was Thessalonica; also included the city of Philippi 1 mediator someone who goes between two people or groups of people 10 Messiah (Hebrew) anointed one. The Greek word is Christ . In Colossians, putting on new clothes meant a) putting on robes of righteousness. b) spending money on quality items. c) showing concern for appearances. d) showing compassion and humility. 17. Which book specifically shows how the gospel works in society? a) Ephesians b) Philemon c) Philippians d) Galatians 18. Timothy’s report to Paul regarding the Thessalonians included a) praise for their faith and love. b) warnings about false teachers. c) sorrow for their shallow faith. d) praise for their generous giving. 19. #### 13.3.2 — Identify some of the key contrasts in Revelation.

Explain John’s use of symbols and characters in Revelation.

Symbols in Revelation

Earlier, we noted that apocalyptic writings speak through symbols. God may have inspired John to use symbols to protect Christians since these symbols were discerned and understood only by believers. The enemies of Jesus could not use His parables to condemn Him. Likewise, the enemies of believers could not use Revelation to condemn believers.

However, John also used symbols for a greater reason: to give us word pictures that add emotion and value to truth. For instance, in Revelation 1:12–20, John could have simply said that Jesus walked among the seven churches. Yet using the symbol of a lampstand instead of the word church gives us a picture. The lampstand reminds us that the church is in the world to shine light in the darkness. In another example, John could have said that an evil leader would rise to rule the world. However, he used the symbol of a beast to emphasize how vile a leader the Antichrist will be. Again, instead of simply contrasting the church with a worldly system, John used the symbols of a pure bride and a harlot to express the contrast more vividly (Wiersbe 1989, 567). Symbols communicate truth in a powerful, emotional way.

It is important to allow Revelation to explain its own symbols when possible. The parables we understand best today are the ones Jesus explained. In the same way, the symbols we understand best in Revelation are the ones John explained to us. Characters in the Story or Drama of Revelation

We have already noted many of the characters in Revelation. The following list summarizes most of them:

Jesus Christ: The book reveals Him as: One “like a son of man” (1:13; 14:14), the “Lamb” (Revelation 6:5–6), the “Lion” (Revelation 5:5), a “male child” (Revelation 12:5), the Rider on the white horse (Revelation 19:11), and the One on the great white throne (Revelation 20:11).

God the Father: He is seated on the throne (Revelation 4:1–11) and referred to throughout the narrative.

The Holy Spirit: He is referred to as the sevenfold Spirit of God (Revelation 1:4; 4:5; 5:6). John was in the Spirit on the Lord’s Day (Revelation 1:10). The Spirit speaks to the seven churches (Revelation 2:1–3:22) and is active throughout the book.

The author John: He sees the visions and narrates the events for us (Revelation 1:9–19). Also, he often shares his feelings and responses to the visions.

The seven churches: Jesus speaks to these churches in Revelation 1–3, and they remain in the background for the rest of the book. All of Revelation was written for these churches and the churches they represent.

Satan: He is the main enemy in Revelation and is referred to as the devil, Satan, and the dragon (Revelation 12:3–13:1; 20:1–10).

The four creatures: These appear often (Revelation 4:6, 8; 5:6, 8, 14; 6:1, 6; 7:11; 14:3; 15:7; 19:4) and may represent all of creation.

The twenty-four elders: The elders may represent all whom God has redeemed (Revelation 4:4, 10; 5:8; 11:16; 19:4).

Angels: Angels are active throughout the book. An angel brought the revelation to John (Revelation 1:1). They worship God and the Lamb (Revelation 4–5), declare judgment (Revelation 10:1–20), and fight in heavenly warfare (Revelation 12). They blow the seven trumpets (Revelation 8:2) and pour out the seven bowls and seven plagues (Revelation 15–16). An angel, perhaps the one of Revelation 1:1, showed John many things (Revelation 22:8).

The two witnesses: These dress in clothes of mourning and call sinners to repent. They prophesy and declare God’s judgment (Revelation 11).

The Antichrist and beast: The Antichrist is the ruler of the beast, which is his kingdom. Sometimes John refers to the Antichrist as the beast because a king and his kingdom are one. The beast has seven heads and ten horns (Revelation 13). Five of these heads were in the past (Revelation 17:10); we believe that they represent the world kingdoms of Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Medo-Persia, and Greece. The sixth head of the beast—Rome—was present in John’s day. We believe that the seventh head is a revised form of the Roman Empire. The Antichrist is the horn that arises to rule over it. The ten horns on the head of the seventh beast are ten kings who reign a short time with the Antichrist (Cole and McGhee 2000, 200–229).

The false prophet: This person represents the Antichrist as the Holy Spirit represents Christ. Satan, the Antichrist, and the false prophet form an unholy triad (Revelation 16:13).

The harlot: John tells us that the harlot is the capital city of the Antichrist (Revelation 17:18) and represents the world and its values. In John’s day, this capital city was Rome. John referred to it as Babylon to protect believers. Although Caesar was considered to be the Antichrist in John’s day, we believe a final Antichrist will arise and rule the world from a great city.

The bride: The bride is the church, the body of Christ (Revelation 19:7–8). The bride includes those who are caught up in the Rapture (1 Thessalonians 4:13–18) and all those saved during the Great Tribulation (Revelation 7:9–17). The bride is united with Christ when He comes to conquer evil.

The many other characters in Revelation include Jezebel (Revelation 2:20–23), the riders on horses (Revelation 6:5–8), the woman (Revelation 12), the martyrs, kings, merchants, sailors, followers of the beast, faithful witnesses of the Lord, slaves, rich and poor people, the 144,000, a great multitude in white robes, all the dead who came to life, and people on thrones. In addition, Revelation describes things and creatures who act like humans: An eagle cries with a loud voice (Revelation 8:13). The earth opens its mouth (Revelation 12:16). An altar responds to God (Revelation 16:7). The new Jerusalem comes as a bride (Revelation 21:9–10). Finally, death and Hades are judged like God’s other enemies. Thus, Revelation has a great and varied list of characters that all play a part in the story of God’s final victory over evil.

**Q:** Identify two possible reasons why John used symbols.

**A:** John may have used symbols to protect Christians and to give us word pictures that add emotion and value to truth.

**Q:** What are two examples that show that symbols give us powerful pictures?

**A:** Possible examples include these: The lampstand reminds us that the church is to shine light to a dark world. The beast emphasizes the kind of leader the Antichrist will be. The bride and harlot contrast the church and the worldly system.

**Q:** Identify at least three contrasts in Revelation 1–5 that describe God’s character or nature.

**A:** Any three of the following: Dependable vs. undependable; holy Trinity vs. evil triad; holy and eternal God vs. evil and temporary beast; Creator vs. created; Lamb who alone is worthy vs. everyone else who is unworthy.

**Q:** What are your favorite three contrasts from Revelation 6–18? Why?

It stands for all who love the world (see 1 John 2:15–17). 1 believe to trust; to consider true; to have a firm conviction 3 chosen lady refers to the church. John may have used this term because believers were being persecuted 11 christocentric focusing directly and primarily on Christ 4 Colossian heresy the false teachings in Colossae that centered on rules, self-denial, worshiping angels, lowering Christ, and claims of new philosophy 7 coming of the Lord also called the Second Coming ; refers to either Christ’s private return (the Rapture) or His public return 8 contend to fight, wrestle, confront, or battle 12 Crete an island southeast of Corinth in the Mediterranean Sea 9 Dalmatia a Roman province northwest of Macedonia. Today, this area includes Serbia and Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Slovenia, Macedonia, and Croatia. 9 Damascus the capital city of Syria, about 150 miles (242 km) north of Jerusalem and about halfway between Jerusalem and Tarsus. Damascus was famous for business. 5 epilogue the concluding section of a letter, play, or piece of music 3 filled with the Spirit also called “baptized with the Spirit”; an experience after conversion with the outward, biblical evidence of speaking in a new language 4 firstborn the first child born to a family, who received special rights and privileges because of birth order. Jesus is called the firstborn because He is first in rank. He is above all that He created. 7 futurist a view that focuses mostly on the future to interpret Revelation. It teaches that Revelation 4–22 will happen in the future. 13 Galatia a province that included cities such as Pisidian, Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe 4 General Epistles the seven letters about Hebrews that are named for their authors. All of them except 2 and 3 John are written to the church; that is, they are not written to a specific church. 1 Gnosticism the teachings of the Gnostics. Gnostic false teachers claimed to have secret knowledge for salvation and taught that the body and all matter were evil. 11 Greeks a people who, under Alexander the Great and his generals, ruled from 330–166 BC and spread their language and culture across the world 1 harlot a prostitute; in Revelation, a symbol of Rome and the people with her values. The harlot represents all who love the world (see 1 John 2:15–17). 13 high priest the most important religious leader of Israel who entered the inner part of the temple once a year to make a sacrifice for the nation’s sin 1 historicist a view that focuses on the past and present to interpret Revelation. It matches Revelation with events of history from the early church to the present. 13 idealist a view that says Revelation is about spiritual ideas, not real people or events. It interprets Revelation like a parable that did not and will not happen. 13 Jerome a Catholic Church leader who made a list of books in the Apocrypha and translated the Bible into Latin. This famous translation is called the Vulgate. 12 Jews those from the twelve tribes of Israel. A Person who is not a Jew is called a Gentile . 1 Jewish Teachers Jewish believes who taught that all believers must practice circumcision for Gentiles 5 Judea the southern region of ancient Palestine, just north of the region of Idumea 4 justification God’s counting an individual as righteous 5 kingdom of heaven the place where the King reigns. On earth, this is in the hearts of believers. The kingdom of heaven has an invisible and a visible phase. 2 Lamb a title of Jesus emphasizing that He became the sacrifice to take away our sins 13 life as used in John, eternal life. Life results from believing in Christ. 3 Macedonia a province in northern Greece whose capital was Thessalonica; also included the city of Philippi 1 mediator someone who goes between two people or groups of people 10 Messiah (Hebrew) anointed one. The Greek word is Christ . The Jews believed that God would send a Messiah to deliver them. 2 parousia (Greek) refers to the coming of Christ at the end of this age 8 perseverance determination not to give up; resolution to continue in spite of hard situations 10 Pharisees literally, the separate people; members of a Jewish group who strictly followed the law of Moses and Jewish religious customs. 1 predestine to choose in advance; to determine the destiny of something before it happens 7 prejudice hatred or hostility toward someone who has different characteristics (usually based on skin color or religion) 4 preterist a view that focuses on the past to interpret Revelation and teaches that Revelation 1–18 happened in the first century 13 prologue the opening section of a letter, play, or piece of music (like an introduction) 3 Pseudepigrapha a group of books written between the Old and New Testaments 12 reconcile to bring into agreement; to settle differences 6 righteousness state of being right with God and doing what is right; a gift of God based on Christ’s death 5 Romans people who conquered the Greeks and ruled from 63 BC to AD 486 from the western end of the Mediterranean Sea to the Euphrates River in the East 1 Sadducees a group of powerful Jewish leaders that included the high priest and the leading officials of the Sanhedrin. They did not believe in the resurrection, angels, or spirits. 1 Samaria the biblical area between Galilee and Judea. (A city called Samaria was also in this region.) The Samaritans were only partly Jewish and therefore hated by the Jews. 4 sanctuary a holy or sacred place; usually refers to a place of worship 10 sign John’s word for miracle; a miracle showing that Jesus is the Messiah 3 Son of Man a named that Jesus called himself, emphasizing that He was both God and man at the same time 1 tetrarch ruler over a fourth of a province; a subordinate ruler 1 theocentric relating to God; focusing on the idea of God 4 Theophilus a common Greek name meaning “lover of God”; addressee of Luke and Acts 4 Akin, Daniel L. 2001. “1, 2, 3 John” . Which group of people built a vast network of ancient roads? a) Romans b) Samaritans c) Greeks d) Jews 2. Which group emphasized oral traditions and believed in an afterlife? a) Romans b) Sadducees c) Pharisees d) Zealots 3. The ultimate center of religious life for the Jews was the a) synagogue. b) Sanhedrin. c) temple. d) local school. 4. One of the standards for a book’s inclusion in the New Testament was its a) early date of writing. b) authorship by an apostle or his associate. c) moral effect on society. d) respected group of recipients. 5. Hebrews is included in the a) letters to all. b) historical books. c) apocalyptic books. d) letters from Paul. 6. Jesus is depicted as the supplier of all our needs in a) Philippians. b) 1 Peter. c) John. d) Colossians. 7. Matthew primarily portrays Jesus as the a) Servant of the Lord. b) Alpha and Omega. c) Son of Man. d) Messiah. 8. To fulfill his purpose, Matthew primarily used a) miracles that Jesus performed. b) quotes from the Old Testament. c) parables the Lord taught. d) a genealogy of Jesus Christ. 9. One of the teaching segments in Matthew is the a) eight parables (chapter. 13). b) ten miracles (chapters 8–9). c) conflict with Jewish leaders (chapters 14–17). d) record of Jesus’ early life (chapters 1–2). 10. Matthew’s gospel emphasized what subject? a) The Passion Week b) The kingdom of heaven c) Jesus as the Son of God d) Jesus’ background 11. The theme of Mark is Jesus as a) the Messiah. b) a Servant. c) the Savior. d) the Word of God. 12. Luke’s gospel emphasized a) Jesus’ teachings. b) Jesus’ miracles. c) Old Testament Scriptures. d) Jesus’ attitude toward prayer. 13. Which of these is found only in Luke’s Gospel? a) Thomas’ doubts about Jesus’ resurrection b) Satan’s temptation of Jesus c) Jesus’ washing of the disciples’ feet d) The Parable of the Good Samaritan 14. Jesus taught in parables because a) He did not have time to prepare a sermon. b) all Jewish teachers taught that way. c) His listeners were poorly educated. d) it was effective in teaching about the Kingdom. 15. The invisible phase of the Kingdom refers to the a) spiritual rule of God. b) period of the Tribulation. c) secret rapture of the church. d) millennial reign of Christ. 16. Jesus demonstrated that He was the Messiah through His a) disciples. b) parentage. c) miracles. d) education. 17. John did not include parables in his Gospel because a) he did not like stories. b) his readers could not understand them. c) his emphasis was to show Christ’s deity. d) he wanted to focus on the Great Commission. 18. John used the word signs to describe a) miracles that Christ performed. b) eternal life through Christ. c) events of the last days. d) belief in Christ. 19. In John’s introduction, the main action is a) manifestation of the Word. b) conflict. c) sanctification. d) belief. 20. The seven “I am” statements of Jesus in John’s Gospel a) provide important evidence supporting the deity of Christ. b) were not related to God’s name in the Old Testament. c) were intended literally, not symbolically. d) were written to the seven churches in Asia. 21. In the Gospel of John, Peter’s life shows us that Jesus a) satisfies all who believe in Him. b) knows our inner thoughts. c) expects us to drink from His cup. d) changes our character as we believe in Him. 22. The best title for the book of Acts is The Acts of a) Some of the Apostles. b) the Holy Spirit. c) the Apostle Paul. d) All of the Apostles. 23. What book traces the growth and history of the early church? a) Matthew b) Mark c) John d) Acts 24. The spread of the gospel in Judea and Samaria is described in Acts a) 1–7. b) 17–28. c) 8–12. d) 13–16. 25. Persecution caused the church in Acts to a) stop preaching in Jesus’ name. b) decrease because of fear. c) spread outward from Jerusalem. d) hunker down and wait it out. UNIT PROGRESS EVALUATION 2 MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTIONS 1. Paul belonged to the tribe of a) Reuben. b) Benjamin. c) Simeon. d) Judah. 2. Paul was a member of the a) Zealots. b) Sadducees. c) Pharisees. d) Essenes. 3. Which of Paul’s letters focus primarily on eschatology? a) 1 and 2 Thessalonians b) 1 and 2 Timothy and Titus c) Romans, Galatians, and 1 and 2 Corinthians d) Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon 4. Romans 4–5 teaches that justification is the a) expression of righteousness. b) opposite of sanctification. c) essence of righteousness. d) provision for righteousness. 5. Paul wrote Galatians to a) express his anger toward the Galatian churches. b) explain justification by faith. c) warn the people about Gnosticism. d) explain the signs of the times. 6. Paul told the Galatians that the gospel was true because a) it is the power of God unto salvation. b) the Jerusalem Council had voted to accept it. c) angels had given it to him. d) it works in personal experience. 7. Paul ministered in Corinth for approximately a) 18 months. b) 24 months. c) 12 months. d) 6 months. 8. The main question of 1 Corinthians 12–14 related to a) spiritual gifts. b) the resurrection of the dead. c) head coverings. d) divorce and remarriage. 9. Paul changed his mind about traveling to Corinth because he a) had urgent business in Macedonia. b) wanted to take an offering to Jerusalem. c) did not want to hurt the believers in Corinth. d) became very sick while preaching in Ephesus. 10. Paul differed from the false apostles in that he a) emphasized the seen and the temporal. b) took pride in the outward appearance of ministry. c) took pride in what was in the heart. d) relied on humans to recommend him. 11. On his third missionary journey, Paul ministered in Ephesus for a) more than four years. b) at least three years. c) about two years. d) about eighteen months. 12. In Ephesians 2–3, Paul discusses the relationship a) of Christians to evil spirits. b) between humanity and God. c) between husband and wife. d) between Jews and Gentiles. 13. The city of Philippi was a) located on the Aegean Sea. b) the site of Paul’s first church. c) a colony made up mostly of women. d) named after Philip the evangelist. 14. Having joy in the midst of trials is the theme of a) Philippians. b) Philemon. c) Ephesians. d) Galatians. 15. One characteristic of the Colossian heresy was a) displaying drunkenness. b) lowering the status of Christ. c) engaging in immorality. d) refusing to meet on the Sabbath. 16. In Colossians, putting on new clothes meant a) putting on robes of righteousness. b) spending money on quality items. c) showing concern for appearances. d) showing compassion and humility. 17. Which book specifically shows how the gospel works in society? a) Ephesians b) Philemon c) Philippians d) Galatians 18. Timothy’s report to Paul regarding the Thessalonians included a) praise for their faith and love. b) warnings about false teachers. c) sorrow for their shallow faith. d) praise for their generous giving. 19. Paul encouraged the Thessalonians by reminding them of a) Paul’s release from prison. b) the suffering of other believers. c) Christ’s second coming. d) a generous offering they would soon receive. 20. We believe that the public phase of Christ’s second coming will occur a) after the Millennium. b) during the Tribulation. c) before the Tribulation. d) after the Tribulation. 21. The term disciple may indicate that Timothy became a Christian a) while Paul was in Rome. b) while Paul was in Ephesus. c) during Paul’s first missionary journey. d) during Paul’s second missionary journey. 22. One of Paul’s main topics in 1 Timothy is a) the second coming of Christ. b) the question of circumcision. c) the use of spiritual gifts in the church. d) instructions about public worship. 23. In Titus, Paul taught that circumcision a) has no religious value. b) is for Jewish believers only. c) should follow salvation. d) is a sign of the new covenant. 24. In 2 Timothy, Paul compares Timothy to an athlete who must a) endure suffering. b) obey the rules of the game. c) finish the race. d) fight the good fight of faith. 25. Paul tells Timothy that all Scripture a) includes the books of the New Testament. b) is profitable, because it would become a best seller. c) should be used to teach, rebuke, correct, and train. d) was written by the finger of God. Most biblical scholars do not believe Paul was the author of Hebrews because a) the author appears to be a second-generation Christian. b) the author does not identify himself. c) Paul was called only to the Gentiles. d) Paul often quoted from the Septuagint. 2. The primary theme of Hebrews is that Jesus is a) superior. b) faithful. c) sovereign. d) righteous. 3. According to Hebrews, if believers keep ignoring God’s warnings, they a) lose rewards in heaven. b) spend time in purgatory. c) miss God’s fullest blessings. d) lose their salvation. 4. Which book is one of the General Epistles? a) Titus b) Revelation c) Hebrews d) James 5. The author of James was most likely a) the son of Alphaeus. b) the Lord’s half-brother. c) a king from Britain. d) John’s brother. 6. Which epistle claims that temptations come from the within? a) James b) 2 Peter c) 1 John d) Jude 7. Peter’s brother was a) Andrew. b) Silas. c) James. d) John. 8. First Peter teaches that trials a) purify our faith. b) are a result of sin. c) are caused by Satan. d) are a means of grace. 9. Believers should be characterized by a) slander. b) meddling. c) humble obedience. d) pride. 10. To counter the Gnostic idea that the body was evil and the spirit good, John showed that a) only what comes out of a person defiles him or her. b) both the body and the spirit are evil. c) Jesus came in the flesh but was sinless. d) all things are pure to the pure. 11. According to 1 John, having love for our brother indicates that we a) have a rich brother. b) have acquired secret knowledge. c) are eternally secure. d) are God’s children. 12. Which concept is found in John, 1 John, and 2 John? a) John refers to himself as “the elder. b) The first will be last, and the last will be first. c) We show love for Jesus by obeying His command to love others. d) Walking in the truth is praiseworthy. 13. Which epistle shows that love and truth must go together? a) Hebrews b) 2 John c) 1 Peter d) 1 John 14. Third John says that Demetrius a) was a silversmith. b) walked in the truth. c) loved to be first. d) had a good reputation. 15. According to 2 Peter, growing in grace requires a) faithful church attendance. b) lots of effort. c) praying in tongues. d) secret knowledge. 16. According to 2 Peter, false teachers a) make Christians stronger. b) target weak or new believers. c) respect authority. d) compare to wells full of water. 17. The author of Jude was most likely a) James and John’s brother. b) a deacon in the early church. c) Jesus’ half-brother. d) one of the twelve disciples. 18. An official church council approved the list of New Testament books around AD a) 167 b) 267 c) 367 d) 467 19. John addressed Revelation to the seven churches in a) Galatia. b) Macedonia. c) Judea. d) Asia. 20. Revelation unveils a) all the details of the future. b) Jesus in His glory. c) the identity of the two witnesses. d) the mystery of godliness. 21. The futurist view teaches that Revelation 4-22 a) is about spiritual ideas, not real people. b) was fulfilled in the first century. c) is fulfilled through church history. d) will be fulfilled in the future. 22. In Revelation 1:19, the phrase “what you have seen” refers to a) John’s vision of Christ. b) the entire collective vision of Revelation. c) all that John had seen during his ministry. d) Christ’s life and ministry. 23. In Revelation, Jesus is NOT described as a) a lion. b) an eagle. c) a shepherd. d) a lamb. 24. John used symbols in Revelation to a) add emotion to the truth. b) keep his readers’ attention. c) pass the time on the Island of Patmos. d) engage in a popular writing style. 25.
